# A uniform OC region near equality in parity mass expansion

This is a conditional regime theorem, not unrestricted OC. Its constant
depends only on the intrinsic fiber dimension, not on n or the number
of fibers. the contributor proof; independent audit pending.

Let S=C intersect(Z^n times R^d) be as in the task, q=dim_H(S), and
M=H_q(S)>0. For a parity class r let M_r be the H_q mass of its positive
q-dimensional fibers and a_r their largest fiber mass. If M_r>0 put

    Delta_r=M-2M_r+a_r.

The arithmetic peak-Bonnesen theorem gives Delta_r>=0. For every q>=1
there is eta_q>0 such that

    Delta_r<=eta_q a_r                              (1)

for some class implies OC. In fact when n>=1 there is one y in S with

    depth_S(y)>= (3/5) gamma_q > (1/2)gamma_q.        (2)

Since gamma_q>=gamma_d and2^(-n)<=1/2, this proves the required OC
constant in this regime. For n=0 use ordinary Grünbaum directly.
For q=0 the separate choice eta_0=1/4 implies OC by counting, as proved
in Section6; the stronger bound(2) is not claimed for q=0.

## 1. An elementary compact stability lemma for one midpoint

For each integer q>=1 there is sigma_q in(0,1/2] such that, whenever
q-dimensional convex bodies A,B satisfy

    1-sigma_q<=|A|,|B|<=1,
    |(A+B)/2|<=1+sigma_q,

some translation B+u has

    |A intersect(B+u)|>=3/4.                        (3)

Here all volumes are in one common q-dimensional Euclidean space.
We give the compactness proof, including the normalization. If the lemma
failed, choose sigma tending to zero and counterexample pairs. Put
D=(A+B)/2. Choose a maximum-volume simplex in D and send it by an affine
map to T=conv(0,e_1,...,e_q). The maximum exists by compactness of the
vertex tuple set and is positive. If x belongs to normalized D, replacing
one vertex of T by x shows every barycentric coordinate of x has absolute
value at most one. Thus

    T subset D' subset[-1,1]^q.

The determinant factors of these maps stay bounded above and below:
|D'| lies between1/q! and2^q, while |D| tends to one. Choose a point in
each normalized input and translate each input separately to contain
zero. Both translated inputs then lie in2(D'-D'), because their widths
are bounded by those of twice D'. They lie in one fixed compact box.

Pass to Hausdorff convergent subsequences of the two inputs and to a
convergent subsequence of the determinant factors. This compactness can
be seen by taking a uniformly convergent subsequence of their uniformly
bounded, uniformly Lipschitz support functions. The limiting volumes
are equal and positive, and their Minkowski average has that same volume.
Volume is continuous under convex Hausdorff convergence: outer parallel
bodies give the upper limit; a full-dimensional limit contains uniform
inner homothetic approximations, giving the lower limit. A lower-dimensional
limit would have outer-neighborhood volumes tending to zero and is excluded
by the positive volume bound.

Equality in ordinary Brunn--Minkowski makes the two limits translates,
because their volumes agree. Translate the second sequence by that fixed
limiting displacement. Both inputs now converge to the same convex body
K of positive volume. Their intersections converge in volume to |K|:
for any fixed interior point of K, both contain its inner homothety
(1-epsilon)K for all sufficiently large indices. Let epsilon tend to
zero, using the corresponding outer containment for the upper bound.
Undoing the maps and translations gives intersections of volume tending
to one, contradicting their asserted bound below3/4. This proves(3).

## 2. Fixing a positive regime constant

With sigma=sigma_q from Section1 choose

    eta_q=(1/2) min{1/4, 2^(-q-1), sigma/2^q,
                      2^(1-q)[(1+sigma)^(1/q)-1]}.

It is strictly positive. If Delta<=eta_q a and epsilon=2^q eta_q, then

    eta_q<2^(1-q), eta_q<=1/4, epsilon<=1/2,
    epsilon<=sigma, eta_q<=sigma,
    (1+epsilon/2)^q<=1+sigma.                        (4)

No asymptotic notation or unspecified smallness condition is used after
this choice. The existence of sigma was proved in Section1.

## 3. The positive class is a nearly equal primitive chain

Use the intrinsic version of
`candidate 670310a99fe94843`. If the positive
bases of the chosen class had affine rank s>=2, it would give

    Delta>=s2^(-q)a>=2^(1-q)a,

contrary to(1) and(4). For rank zero there is only one positive class
fiber, M_r=a, and M=a+Delta<=(1+eta_q)a. Its ordinary intrinsic centroid
therefore has depth at least gamma_q/(1+eta_q)>=4 gamma_q/5. This gives
(2) for n>=1, and handles this case.

In rank one, let the class have N>=2 bases. Positive fibers are convexly
complete within the residue lattice, so their bases are

    p_0+2j v, j=0,...,N-1,

for a primitive integer vector v. Put L=N-1. The rank-one path formula
in the same triangulation note gives

    Delta>=2^(-q)(a-b),                              (5)

where b is the smallest class fiber volume. Indeed the volume-root
sequence is concave, so its minimum is at an endpoint. A maximum root
at an endpoint gives the bracket a minus the other endpoint's volume;
an internal maximum gives twice a minus the two endpoint volumes, which
is at least a-b. Thus every class volume belongs to[(1-epsilon)a,a].

All integer bases p_0+j v,0<=j<=2L, have positive q-volume fibers. For
intrinsic q, their direction spaces agree with those of the class:
the latter are parallel by the integer-midpoint dimension argument, and
each intervening integer fiber contains a positive q-dimensional
interpolation of them and has dimension at most q. We work in that
common q-dimensional direction space when comparing these fibers.

## 4. Bounding the actual middle fiber and aligning the endpoints

Write f_j for the q-th root of the fiber volume at p_0+j v. This sequence
is concave by convexity and q-dimensional Brunn--Minkowski. On the even
indices, (5) gives

    B:=((1-epsilon)a)^(1/q)<=f_(2j)<=A:=a^(1/q).

If N>=3, every odd index j has an even index two steps beyond one of
its neighboring even indices. Concavity at that neighboring even index
(with weights2/3 and1/3) gives

    f_j <=(3A-B)/2 <=A(1+epsilon/2).

For the first interval use the even indices2 and4; for the last interval
use the two even indices on its left. The inequality
(1-epsilon)^(1/q)>=1-epsilon justifies the second bound. Thus, whether
the middle index L is odd or even, its volume is at most(1+sigma)a
by(4). If N=2, the middle volume is at most

    M-M_r=M_r-a+Delta<=a+Delta<=(1+sigma)a,

because M_r is the sum of its two endpoint volumes, each at most a.
This remains valid when other fibers outside the chain carry mass.

Let A_0,A_1 be the two extreme fibers of this chain. Translate them into
their common direction space and scale volumes by a. Their volumes lie
in[1-epsilon,1], and their Minkowski midpoint is contained in the actual
middle fiber, whose volume is at most1+sigma. Section1 therefore gives
a relative translation for which their intersection K has volume

    H_q(K)>=3a/4.                                   (6)

An affine shear in the continuous coordinates, leaving all integer
coordinates fixed, performs this translation at the last endpoint and
zero translation at the first. On the line its coefficient increases
linearly from zero to one. Convexity then makes EVERY intervening
integer fiber contain the same K. Translations within fibers preserve
H_q, even for any outside fibers with different direction spaces.
The normalization in Section1 was only used to prove existence of the
relative translation; it is undone before this shear is applied.

## 5. One actual point, all halfspaces, and the mass comparison

The transformed source contains the product of the odd-length chain
p_0+jv,0<=j<=2L, with K. Choose its middle base p_0+Lv and the ordinary
intrinsic centroid g of K. Pulling back by the shear gives one point of
the original S.

Use the complete, independently audited paired-centroid-tail theorem
`candidate 732b11a769399016`: for a convex
q-body K centered at g, its normalized parallel cap function satisfies
F(t)+F(-t)>=2 gamma_q for all t>=0. Its proof and exact localization
dependency are contained in that source; the independent audit is
`unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)`.

For any ambient halfspace through the chosen point with nonzero
continuous restriction to the direction space of K, the thresholds in
each opposite pair of retained fibers are opposite. Each pair contributes
at least2 gamma_q |K|, and the middle contributes gamma_q |K|. If that
continuous restriction is zero, the middle fiber and at least one of each
pair are wholly contained, giving (L+1)|K|>=gamma_q(2L+1)|K|. These
arguments include oblique normals, normals transverse to the intrinsic
direction space, and closed halfspaces carrying full-fiber boundary mass.
A containing halfspace can first be translated to pass through the point.

The resulting raw depth is at least gamma_q(2N-1)|K|. On the other hand

    M=2M_r-a+Delta <=(2N-1)a+eta_q a.

Using(6) and eta_q<=1/4 gives

    (2N-1)|K|/M >=(3/4)/(1+eta_q/(2N-1)) >=3/5.

This proves(2). The selected point lies in the retained K in an original
integer fiber, so it is not an averaged point outside S. Monotonicity
gamma_q>=gamma_d for q<=d, together with n>=1, proves OC in this regime.
For n=0 the convex-body assumption makes q=d and ordinary Grünbaum applies.

## 6. Counting case

If q=0, every nonempty convex integer fiber is one point. Thus a_r=1
and Delta_r=M-2M_r+1 is a nonnegative integer by the sumset count. The
condition Delta_r<=eta_0=1/4 makes it zero. The Ehrhart-level count excludes
rank at least two, since its excess over2N-1 is then at least one. Rank
zero gives a single point. In rank one the positive class is a consecutive
residue-lattice chain, and its2N-1 intervening integer fibers exhaust S.
Convexity and their zero-dimensionality make their continuous coordinates
affine along the chain. Its middle point lies in S, and every closed
containing halfspace captures at least N of these points. Its depth is
N/(2N-1)>1/2, proving OC because n>=1 in this case. No root exponent or
undefined0^0 is used.

The unproved global step is to handle bodies whose EVERY positive parity
class has Delta_r>eta_q a_r. The present theorem does not infer that some
class meets(1), and does not settle that complementary regime.
